outline.description: Sets out who the parties are, how premium financing worked, what happened to the policies, the claims asserted, and how the case reached the Fifth Circuit on cross-motions for summary judgment focused on statutory compliance.
subtopics: Parties: Former insureds Kimberly Williams and Felita Wright; third-party accident victim Nicholas Jenkins; insurer GoAuto; premium finance company APAC
Premium finance agreements: APAC pays full premium; insureds repay in installments; APAC holds power of attorney to cancel on default
Events: Nonpayment by insureds; APAC sent 10-day default notices; APAC initiated cancellation; GoAuto processed cancellations
Claims: Ineffective cancellation under Louisiana law; misrepresentation; breach of good faith and fair dealing

Procedural path: State-court class action; removal to M.D. La.; cross-motions for summary judgment limited to statutory compliance; district court grants GoAuto’s motion and dismisses all claims with prejudice; appeal by Williams, Wright, and Jenkins

outline.chapter_title: Louisiana’s Premium Finance Cancellation Framework and Strict Compliance
outline.description: Explains the governing statute and the jurisprudence demanding strict adherence, setting the legal yardstick for evaluating GoAuto/APAC’s procedures.
subtopics: Core statute: La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) permits a premium finance company to request cancellation by mail, private carrier, or email, sending the notice of cancellation with a statement certifying (i) valid power of attorney, (ii) uncured default, (iii) prior notice to insured with date sent, and (iv) notice to interested parties
Insurer’s action upon receipt: § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) – once the insurer receives the notice and certification, cancellation has been requested and the insurer may proceed to cancel
Strict adherence doctrine: Louisiana courts require exact compliance; any defect renders cancellation ineffective (Delatte v. Lemotte; Eaglin v. Champion Ins. Co.)
Rationale for strictness: Fixes precise date/time of cancellation and preserves minimum cure period (Britten v. Reavis)

Prior case treatments of “certifying”: References to a required “statement certifying compliance” without discussing signatures (KMJ Servs., Inc. v. Hood; Hodges v. Colonial Lloyd’s Ins.; Lewis v. Julien); Benitez v. Elsayed notes absence of signature as one shortcoming but does not hold a signature is independently required

outline.description: Details the factual record of how APAC and GoAuto implemented cancellations, including automated and post-processing steps, as the basis for analyzing statutory compliance.
subtopics: APAC 10-day notices: Default notice to insured warning of cancellation if no payment within ten days; notices to interested parties per finance agreement

Automated request: If no cure by the tenth day at midnight, APAC’s system emails GoAuto a copy of the cancellation notice and a certification request on APAC letterhead stating the four required items
Immediate system action: GoAuto’s web service receives the email/API call and automatically cancels the policy upon receipt; no human involvement at that moment

Post-cancellation paperwork: Later that morning, an APAC employee applies a signature stamp to printed cancellation documents; physical handling varied over time (pre-2017 shared cabinet; since 2017, documents taken to a GoAuto employee who stamps “received” and files), with plaintiffs contesting whether the stamper was APAC’s employee

District court’s alternative rationale: Treated APAC’s physical delivery as use of a “private carrier”; Fifth Circuit notes lack of Louisiana authority and does not reach this ground because email receipt sufficed

outline.chapter_title: Issues on Appeal and the Court’s Analysis: Signature and Receipt
outline.description: Analyzes the two central statutory questions—whether certification requires a signature and what constitutes insurer “receipt”—and applies them to affirm summary judgment for GoAuto.
subtopics: Issue 1: Does “certifying” under § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) require a signature? Statute is silent; certification is by the company, not a named individual; Louisiana cases do not impose a signature requirement; Benitez criticized a notice lacking both identification and certification but did not hold a signature is independently necessary

Holding on certification: Strict adherence does not permit courts to add a signature requirement absent statutory text; APAC’s statements on company letterhead certifying all four elements satisfy the statute without a pre-cancellation signature

Issue 2: Did GoAuto have “receipt” of the cancellation request before cancelling? Statute lacks a definition; court adopts Black’s Law Dictionary definitions of “receipt/receive” as taking possession/custody

Electronic receipt suffices: GoAuto’s system’s immediate intake of APAC’s email/web-service call constitutes receipt; modern statutory context accommodates automated, electronic delivery and action; no need for human possession before cancellation

Rejection of plaintiffs’ physical-possession theory: Later application of a signature stamp and disputes about who stamped or filed the paper are immaterial because cancellation followed electronic receipt

Consequences for remaining claims and motions: With statutory compliance established, plaintiffs’ motion for partial summary judgment was properly denied and all claims against GoAuto were correctly dismissed

outline.chapter_title: Certification Request, Disposition, and Practical Significance
outline.description: Addresses the plaintiffs’ request to certify questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, states the final disposition, and distills compliance lessons for insurers and premium finance companies.
subtopics: Certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court: Fifth Circuit’s standard—used sparingly; unsettled state-law terms alone do not warrant certification (Jefferson v. Lead Industries Ass’n); request denied
Disposition: District court’s judgment AFFIRMED; GoAuto’s procedures complied with § 9:3550(G)(3); derivative tort and good-faith claims fail

Practical takeaways: Email and automated web-service receipt can satisfy “receipt”; certification can be by the company without a pre-cancellation signature if the notice expressly certifies all four statutory items; preserve records demonstrating timing and content of electronic transmissions
Boundaries and open questions: Strict compliance remains mandatory; courts will not add extra-textual formalities; the meaning of “private carrier” remains unresolved because unnecessary to decision
